Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- A six-month trial was launched this week that promises to transform the way luggage is tracked and monitored at London's Heathrow airport. As many as 28 in every 1,000 passengers do not arrive at their destination at the same time as their luggage. The trial -- run by BAA and airline Emirates -- is using RFID (radio-frequency identification) technology to tag baggage. This will allow staff to more accurately track bags passing through the airport. The crucial difference between RFID and the existing barcode system is its scanning accuracy. Barcode tags can be easily damaged in transit and are also at risk of being covered when scanned. If not scanned, details must be entered manually into the system, adding time and error to the process. BAA estimates that Heathrow can read only 60 per cent of labels that pass through. RFID is reported to offer over 99 percent accuracy. The £150,000 trial -- the first of its kind in the UK -- will continue for six months tracking bags for passengers traveling with Emirates to and from Dubai, and transferring through Heathrow. A duplicate of the Heathrow system has been installed at Dubai Airport. During the check-in process at Heathrow Terminal 3, staff apply tags containing RFID chips to bags with information including the passenger's name and route. The chips are then read on entry into the baggage system; they are tracked as they move throughout; and finally on leaving the system. As a result, says Shaun Cowlam, Logistics Director at Heathrow Airport, staff can know where a bag is at "every moment of every day". BAA is also considering introducing a SMS text messaging service to keep passengers informed of where their bags are. When passengers arrive at Heathrow, says Cowlam, the idea will be to send passengers a text informing them what belt and what time their bags will arrive at. Ultimately, the use of RFID could extend services to frequent flyers, and provide the means to added value services such as faster check-in, and even be integrated with secure collection and delivery. The main benefits, however, will be for travelers passing through major hubs such as Heathrow and Dubai, as this system offers better processing of baggage on transfer flights. Emirates and BAA are sharing the costs of the trial. But as Vic Sheppard, Emirates Vice President for UK and Ireland says, "cost is not an issue", especially considering the savings the airline is expected to achieve by reducing loss and repatriation of bags. And as Cowlam adds: "if we can introduce this across the whole network the costs will reduce significantly." Hong Kong International Airport was one of the first to deploy RFID technology in 2005. But as outlined in a recent survey by SITA, RFID is being used in just 6 percent of the airports surveyed. "For this system to really take off we need other airports and other airlines to embrace the technology," says Cowlam. That widespread adoption may not be far off. The SITA survey indicated that RFID tags will be used in 45 percent of airports by the end of 2009. It's still early days, but BAA and Emirates are optimistic for RFID's future in airports. "There have been giant strides in the technology in aviation in recent years. But in the last few decades there hasn't been any advancement in the methods adopted for baggage handling," says Sheppard. "This is a major step forward." E-mail to a friend .

LONDON, England (CNN) — A new six-month pilot program began this week at London’s Heathrow Airport, with the aim of changing how baggage is followed and managed. Currently, up to 28 out of every 1,000 travelers do not reach their destination at the same time as their bags.

The project, operated by BAA together with Emirates airline, is testing RFID — radio-frequency identification — technology on luggage tags. The system is designed to help airport employees monitor bags moving through Heathrow with far greater precision.

The key advantage of RFID over the barcode labels now in use is the reliability of scanning. Barcode tags may be damaged while bags are being transported, and they can also be obscured at the moment they are scanned. When a barcode cannot be read, workers have to type the information into the system by hand, which slows the process and increases the chance of mistakes. According to BAA, Heathrow is able to read only about 60 percent of the baggage labels that move through the airport. RFID, by contrast, is said to deliver accuracy of more than 99 percent.

The trial, costing £150,000 and described as the first program of its type in the UK, will run for six months. It will track luggage for Emirates passengers flying to and from Dubai, as well as those connecting through Heathrow. A matching version of the Heathrow system has also been set up at Dubai Airport.

At check-in in Heathrow’s Terminal 3, staff attach luggage labels fitted with RFID chips. These chips store details such as the traveler’s name and journey route. The chips are read when the bags enter the baggage-handling system, monitored as they move through it, and read again when they exit. Shaun Cowlam, Heathrow Airport’s logistics director, says this means staff can identify a bag’s location at “every moment of every day.”

BAA is also looking at the possibility of offering passengers SMS updates about the whereabouts of their luggage. Cowlam says that, when passengers land at Heathrow, the plan would be to send them a text message telling them which carousel their bags will appear on and when they are expected to arrive.

In the longer term, RFID could be used to improve services for frequent travelers and support extra features such as quicker check-in, as well as secure baggage collection and delivery. Its biggest advantages, however, are expected to be for people transferring through large hub airports like Heathrow and Dubai, because the technology can make baggage handling on connecting flights more efficient.

Emirates and BAA are dividing the cost of the test. Vic Sheppard, Emirates’ vice president for the UK and Ireland, says that “cost is not an issue,” particularly because the airline expects to save money by cutting the number of lost bags and the expense of returning baggage to passengers. Cowlam adds that if the system can be introduced throughout the entire network, the costs will fall substantially.

Hong Kong International Airport was among the earliest airports to introduce RFID, doing so in 2005. However, a recent SITA survey found that only 6 percent of the airports questioned were using the technology. Cowlam says, “For this system to really take off we need other airports and other airlines to embrace the technology.”

Broader use may be approaching soon. The SITA survey suggested that RFID tags would be in use at 45 percent of airports by the end of 2009.

Although the technology is still in its early stages, BAA and Emirates are confident about RFID’s prospects in airport baggage systems. Sheppard says aviation technology has made “giant strides” in recent years, but that baggage-handling methods have seen little progress over the past several decades. “This is a major step forward,” he says.

**Heathrow tests RFID baggage tags in bid to cut lost luggage**

*London* — London Heathrow Airport is testing radio-frequency identification technology on passenger bags in a six-month trial aimed at reducing mishandled luggage and giving travelers more timely updates on where their bags are.

The trial, run by airport operator BAA in partnership with Emirates, is using RFID baggage tags on selected Emirates flights between Heathrow and Dubai. Unlike conventional barcodes, which must be visible to scanners and can be damaged, folded or obscured during handling, RFID tags can be read wirelessly and do not require a direct line of sight.

Airport officials say that could make a major difference in one of aviation’s most persistent problems: bags that miss connections, are loaded onto the wrong aircraft or are delayed in complex transfer systems.

“Barcode technology has served the industry well, but it has limitations,” a BAA executive said in a statement announcing the trial. “RFID gives us the ability to track bags more reliably at key points in the airport journey and to identify problems before they affect passengers.”

Under the test, RFID-tagged bags are tracked as they move through Heathrow’s baggage system and are integrated with systems at Dubai International Airport, Emirates’ main hub. The Heathrow-Dubai route was selected because of Emirates’ high passenger volumes and Dubai’s role as a major connecting airport for long-haul traffic.

Emirates said the goal is to create a more seamless baggage record across both airports, allowing airline and ground-handling staff to see whether a bag has been accepted, screened, sorted, loaded or transferred.

“For our customers, baggage reliability is a key part of the travel experience,” an Emirates executive said. “By linking Heathrow and Dubai through RFID tracking, we can improve visibility and respond faster if a bag is delayed or misrouted.”

The trial also includes passenger-facing updates. Travelers whose bags are part of the RFID test may receive SMS notifications about baggage status, including confirmation that a bag has been loaded or advice if a bag has been delayed and will be delivered later.

Industry analysts say such messaging could help reduce anxiety at baggage reclaim and cut the number of passengers queuing at airline service desks to ask about missing luggage.

The cost of RFID baggage systems has long been a barrier to widespread adoption. RFID tags are more expensive than standard printed barcode labels, and airports must install readers, software and integration systems throughout baggage halls, loading areas and transfer points. However, supporters argue that the investment can be offset by lower mishandling costs, fewer compensation claims and reduced manual tracing.

Airlines worldwide spend billions of dollars each year dealing with delayed and lost baggage, including the costs of locating bags, transporting them to passengers and staffing service counters. Even small improvements in tracking accuracy can translate into significant savings at large hubs such as Heathrow.

BAA said the six-month test will measure read rates, reliability, operational impact and the cost-benefit case for broader deployment. If successful, the trial could pave the way for wider RFID use across more routes and airlines at Heathrow.

A Heathrow official said the airport is focused on practical results rather than technology for its own sake.

“The test is about proving whether RFID can work at scale in a busy airport environment,” the official said. “If it improves baggage performance and gives passengers better information, it has the potential to become an important part of future airport operations.”

Emirates said Dubai’s participation is central to the project because baggage tracking is only as useful as the network behind it. A bag that can be identified at departure but not at arrival or transfer points still leaves gaps in the passenger journey.

“This is not just about tagging a suitcase,” the Emirates executive said. “It is about building a connected baggage process from check-in to final destination.”

The trial comes as airports and airlines face growing pressure to modernize baggage handling amid rising passenger numbers and increasingly complex international connections. For travelers, the promise is simple: fewer lost bags — and better information when something goes wrong.

**London —** Heathrow Airport has begun testing radio-frequency identification baggage tags with Emirates as part of a trial aimed at reducing lost and mishandled luggage and improving the reliability of baggage tracking across the airport.

The trial, expected to run for **six months**, will see selected Emirates bags fitted with RFID-enabled tags that can be scanned automatically as they move through key points in the baggage system. Unlike traditional barcode tags, which must be visible and aligned with a scanner, RFID tags can be read remotely using radio signals, even when a label is not facing the reader or is partially obscured.

Airport officials say the technology could significantly improve baggage tracking accuracy. Barcode systems typically rely on line-of-sight scanning and can miss bags if labels are folded, damaged, poorly printed or hidden against other luggage. RFID systems, by contrast, are widely reported to achieve read rates of around **99%**, compared with lower accuracy levels for conventional barcode scanning.

For passengers, the potential benefits include fewer misplaced bags, faster identification of luggage during connections and arrivals, and more accurate updates on where a bag is in the airport journey. Improved tracking could also help airlines reunite passengers with delayed luggage more quickly when disruption occurs.

The Heathrow-Emirates test comes as airports and airlines worldwide face pressure to modernize baggage handling, particularly as passenger volumes recover and transfer hubs handle growing numbers of connecting bags. Mishandled luggage remains one of the most frustrating travel problems for passengers and a costly issue for airlines.

However, aviation experts caution that RFID’s full benefits depend on broader adoption across the industry. A tag that can be read at Heathrow is most useful when other airports, airlines and ground handlers on the same journey also have compatible RFID infrastructure. Without wider deployment, tracking gaps can still occur once bags leave airports equipped with the technology.

If the trial proves successful, Heathrow could expand RFID use more widely across its baggage operations. Emirates, which operates major long-haul services from Heathrow, is expected to use the findings to assess how the system could improve baggage performance for passengers travelling through one of the world’s busiest international airports.

## Tiny chips, big change: How RFID is transforming baggage handling at Heathrow

**London (CNN) —** For many air travelers, the moment a suitcase disappears behind the check-in belt is an act of faith. At London Heathrow, one of the world’s busiest international airports, that leap of trust is increasingly being backed by a technology more commonly associated with contactless payments, warehouse logistics and retail inventory: RFID.

Radio-frequency identification chips, embedded in or attached to airline baggage tags, are being used to give bags a more reliable digital identity as they move through Heathrow’s sprawling baggage system. The goal is simple but ambitious: fewer lost bags, faster transfers and better information for airlines and passengers when things go wrong.

### How the system works

Traditional baggage handling relies heavily on printed barcodes attached to luggage at check-in. Those barcodes must be “seen” by optical scanners as bags move through conveyors, sorting machines, security screening and loading areas. But tags can be crumpled, obscured, torn or poorly positioned, making them difficult to scan.

RFID changes that process. Instead of requiring a direct line of sight, an RFID tag contains a tiny chip and antenna that can be read by radio waves. As a suitcase passes through a checkpoint — at check-in, sorting, transfer, loading or arrival — RFID readers detect the tag and capture its unique ID.

That ID is linked to the passenger’s itinerary in the airline’s baggage system, allowing the airport and airline to know where the bag was last detected and where it should go next.

In practice, the technology creates a chain of custody for luggage: accepted at check-in, cleared through security, sorted for the correct flight, loaded onto the aircraft, transferred between flights or delivered to the arrivals hall.

### Why Heathrow matters

Heathrow is a major test case for baggage technology because of its scale and complexity. The airport handles tens of millions of passengers each year and serves as a critical transfer hub, where bags often need to move quickly between terminals, airlines and aircraft.

Transfer bags are among the hardest to manage. A passenger may land from New York and connect onward to Mumbai, Geneva or Edinburgh, with only a narrow window for their suitcase to make the same journey. If a bag misses a scan or is routed to the wrong belt, the error can cascade quickly.

RFID gives baggage systems more opportunities to confirm a bag’s location — and to flag problems earlier.

### What passengers could notice

For travelers, the most visible benefit may be improved baggage tracking through airline apps. Some carriers already allow customers to see when a bag has been checked in, loaded onto the aircraft or delivered at the destination. RFID can make those updates more accurate and more frequent.

It may also reduce the dreaded wait at the carousel. If airlines and airport teams know exactly which bags have arrived, which are still being unloaded and which were left behind, they can provide clearer information instead of leaving passengers staring at an empty belt.

The technology does not make baggage mishandling impossible. Weather disruption, tight connections, staffing shortages and aircraft changes can still create problems. But RFID can make it easier to identify where a failure occurred and recover more quickly.

### Why it could transform baggage handling

Airlines and airports have long viewed baggage as one of aviation’s most expensive operational headaches. Mishandled luggage can require courier delivery, customer service support, compensation and reputational damage. For passengers, a lost suitcase can disrupt holidays, business trips and family visits.

RFID could transform baggage handling because it improves visibility across a system that has historically relied on fragmented data and physical scanning points.

The benefits include:

- **Higher read rates:** RFID tags can be detected without being perfectly aligned with a scanner.  
- **Faster sorting:** Bags can move through automated systems with fewer manual interventions.  
- **Better transfer performance:** Airports can identify bags at risk of missing connections.  
- **Improved accountability:** Airlines can see where a bag was last scanned and which part of the journey failed.  
- **Passenger transparency:** More accurate tracking can be shared through mobile apps and notifications.  

### Part of a wider aviation shift

The move toward RFID comes as the airline industry pushes for more automation and real-time data. The International Air Transport Association has encouraged better baggage tracking across the passenger journey, and many airlines have invested in systems that capture bag status at key points.

RFID is not the only technology being used. Airports and airlines are also experimenting with computer vision, machine learning, Bluetooth tracking, robotics and improved baggage reconciliation systems. Some travelers have taken matters into their own hands by placing consumer trackers such as Apple AirTags or Tile devices inside their luggage.

But RFID has a key advantage: it can be built into the official baggage process, rather than operating as a passenger workaround.

### The future of the suitcase

For Heathrow, RFID is part of a broader effort to make baggage handling more resilient as passenger volumes grow and connections become more complex. The technology may be invisible to most travelers, hidden inside a paper tag or label, but its impact could be significant.

The promise is not just that fewer bags will be lost. It is that bags will become traceable objects in a connected airport ecosystem — scanned, routed and monitored from the check-in desk to the aircraft hold to the arrivals belt.

For passengers, that could mean one less travel anxiety. The suitcase may still vanish behind the rubber flaps at check-in, but increasingly, it will no longer disappear from view.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news piece about BAA and Emirates sharing the cost of a £150,000 RFID luggage-tracking experiment at Heathrow, including SITA survey figures, Hong Kong’s earlier use of RFID, and possible future services like SMS bag notifications.
counterfactuals.output:
**BAA and Emirates to split £150,000 cost of Heathrow RFID baggage trial**

BAA and Emirates are to share the cost of a £150,000 experiment at Heathrow designed to test whether radio-frequency identification technology can make airline baggage handling more reliable and give passengers better information about the whereabouts of their bags.

The trial will use RFID luggage tags on selected Emirates bags travelling through Heathrow, allowing baggage to be identified by radio signal rather than relying solely on conventional bar-code labels. Unlike bar codes, which must be visible to a scanner and can fail if labels are creased, wet, torn or turned the wrong way, RFID tags can be read at a distance and without a direct line of sight.

The project is intended to assess whether RFID can reduce the number of mishandled bags, improve sorting accuracy and provide a more detailed record of each item’s progress through the airport system. BAA, Heathrow’s operator, and Emirates will each contribute half of the £150,000 cost.

The experiment comes as the aviation industry continues to grapple with the financial and reputational cost of lost and delayed luggage. Figures from SITA, the air transport communications and IT specialist, have shown the scale of the problem: tens of millions of bags are mishandled globally each year, costing airlines billions of dollars in tracing, delivery and compensation. SITA’s baggage surveys have also repeatedly identified transfer baggage—bags moving between flights—as one of the most common sources of errors.

Supporters of RFID argue that more accurate tracking could help airlines and airports spot problems earlier, particularly at large hubs such as Heathrow where bags may pass through complex conveyor, sorting and loading systems. If a bag is sent to the wrong make-up area or misses a connection, an RFID-based system could in principle alert staff sooner than existing processes.

Heathrow is not the first major airport to explore the technology. Hong Kong International Airport was among the earlier adopters of RFID baggage tagging, deploying the technology as part of its baggage handling operations before many European hubs had moved beyond trials. Its experience has been closely watched by airlines and airport operators because RFID read rates are generally expected to outperform traditional optical bar-code scanning, especially in high-volume environments.

For Emirates, the Heathrow trial also fits with broader efforts to improve passenger service on long-haul routes. The airline’s operation depends heavily on connecting traffic through its Dubai hub, making reliable baggage handling a key part of the customer experience. A passenger whose bag fails to make a connection may be travelling onwards to another country, increasing the complexity and cost of returning the item.

If the Heathrow experiment proves successful, the technology could eventually support new passenger-facing services. One possibility is sending travellers text-message alerts when their bags have been loaded onto an aircraft, arrived at the destination, or been delayed. Such SMS notifications could reduce anxiety at the carousel and cut the number of enquiries to airline service desks.

However, wider adoption would require investment and coordination across airlines, airports, ground handlers and technology suppliers. RFID tags are more expensive than standard paper bar-code tags, and the greatest benefits are likely to come only when multiple airports on a route can read and exchange baggage data. Industry bodies have also warned that common standards are essential if airlines are to avoid building incompatible systems.

For now, the Heathrow project is a limited test rather than a full-scale rollout. But with passenger numbers rising and airport baggage systems under increasing pressure, BAA and Emirates hope the £150,000 trial will show whether RFID can move from promising technology to practical solution.
